passage:
The hostel room Farida shared with Nandini was so small that their beds touched, and on Tuesday night Nandini's phone call home filled every corner of it. Farida lay facing the wall.
She had submitted her marketing report at 11:58 that morning, two minutes before the portal closed, after another all-nighter. "You are so lazy," she told herself silently. "Useless. Every single time."
She made the vow again, the fourth this semester: from tomorrow, a new timetable, up at six, no phone.
On Wednesday the next assignment came out. Farida opened the brief, and the moment she saw it the voice started again: you'll just mess this one up too. Her chest went tight. She closed the laptop and picked up her phone.
"I'll start after lunch," she told Nandini, who had finally hung up.
By Friday she still hadn't opened it again.

qa.q: What time did Farida submit her marketing report?
qa.a: At 11:58 that morning, two minutes before the portal closed.

qa.q: Why did Farida's chest go tight when she opened the new brief?
qa.a: The harsh voice calling her lazy and predicting she would mess up again made the new task feel threatening before she even began.

qa.q: What could break Farida's loop instead of another vow?
qa.a: Speaking to herself more kindly after a late submission and taking one small step on the new brief, rather than a whole new timetable, would ease the discomfort that keeps her avoiding.

qa.q: What might Nandini notice about Farida this week?
qa.a: Nandini may only see Farida on her phone saying she'll start after lunch, unaware of the harsh voice and the tight chest behind it.

grounding: Shows a student calling herself lazy after a last-minute submission, vowing to change, then avoiding the next task because the harsh self-talk makes it feel worse.

passage:
On the wall above Jatin's desk in the Malviya Nagar flat hung three sheets of paper, each titled NEW ME in thick marker: January, March, and one he had written at 2 am last night after missing the college design competition by a day.
"Nikamma," he muttered at his reflection in the dark laptop screen. "Good-for-nothing. Always the same."
His cousin Ramesh, who shared the flat, came in with two cups of chai. "Another NEW ME?"
"This time I mean it. No more delays."
By Saturday the next task was due: a logo for their uncle's shop. Every time Jatin sat down, the word nikamma sounded in his head, and designing felt heavier than ever. He cleaned the kitchen instead. Twice.
Ramesh watched him scrub the same pan and said quietly, "You're not lazy, yaar. You're scared of that word you keep calling yourself."

qa.q: What title was written on each of the three sheets above Jatin's desk?
qa.a: NEW ME, in thick marker.

qa.q: Why did designing the logo feel heavier than ever to Jatin?
qa.a: Each time he sat down, the word 'nikamma' sounded in his head, so the task carried the sting of his own harsh judgement.

qa.q: What turning point does Ramesh's remark open?
qa.a: It invites Jatin to see that harsh self-talk, not laziness, is making tasks harder, so he could drop the insults and start the logo with one small step.

qa.q: What might Ramesh be feeling as he watches Jatin scrub the same pan?
qa.a: Ramesh seems worried and caring, recognising the pattern of vows and avoidance and wanting Jatin to stop calling himself names.

grounding: Illustrates a young man's cycle of calling himself useless, writing new vows and then avoiding the next task as the self-criticism makes it heavier.

passage:
The PG in Delhi had a power cut every evening, and Noor had just submitted another assignment at the last minute. She lay on her bed in the dark, phone torch pointed at the ceiling.
"You're so lazy," she told herself. "You always do this. What's wrong with you?"
She made a vow: next time, she'd start on day one. She even wrote it on a sticky note.
The next assignment came on Monday. She looked at it and felt the same heaviness, plus something new: dread about failing her own vow. That made it worse. She put it off to Wednesday. Then Friday.
Her roommate Tarun called from the next room, "Noor, you okay?" She didn't answer.

qa.q: Where did Noor write her vow?
qa.a: On a sticky note.

qa.q: What was Noor feeling when she looked at the next assignment?
qa.a: She felt heavy and full of dread, now also afraid of failing her own vow, which made starting even harder.

qa.q: What could break Noor's self-blame loop?
qa.a: Replacing harsh words like "lazy" with kinder, practical ones, and starting with one small step instead of a big vow.

qa.q: What might Tarun be sensing when he calls out?
qa.a: Tarun may sense she is low, and feel concerned, even without knowing why.

grounding: Shows a student calling herself lazy after a last-minute deadline, vowing to change, then repeating the pattern as harsh self-talk adds dread.

passage:
Avni had submitted her report at 11:58 p.m., two minutes before the deadline. Now, in their Pune hostel room, she sat on the floor, hugging her knees.
"I'm such a failure," she told Jasleen. "Lazy. Useless. Every single time."
"You finished it," Jasleen said.
"At 11:58! I swear, next time I'll start the day it's set."
Jasleen had heard the same vow three times this semester.
The next week, a new assignment came. Avni opened it, heard the voice in her head, you'll mess it up, you always do, and closed the laptop. She felt worse than before she'd opened it.

qa.q: What time did Avni submit her report?
What was Avni feeling when she opened the new assignment?
qa.a: She felt worse, weighed down by her own harsh voice saying she'd mess it up, which made closing the laptop feel easier.

qa.q: What could help Avni more than another vow?
qa.a: Talking to herself kindly and starting with a very small first step, perhaps working alongside Jasleen.

qa.q: How might Jasleen feel hearing the same vow again?
qa.a: Jasleen probably feels sympathetic but a bit worried, seeing the vow never changes the pattern.

grounding: Shows a student calling herself lazy and vowing to change after a last-minute deadline, then repeating the pattern as harsh self-talk makes starting harder.

passage:
"Jaya, why are you sitting in the dark?"
"Because I'm useless, Bhupen bhaiya. I submitted my project an hour late. Again."
"You're not useless."
"I'm lazy. I promised myself after the last one. I promised!"
"And the next one?"
"I'll start it tomorrow. First thing. I swear."
"You said that last month."
"Don't!" She pulled her knees up. "I know. I'm the worst. Every time I look at the work I just hear how bad I am."
Bhupen sat down beside her. "Maybe that voice is the problem. Would you talk to your friend like that?"
Jaya was quiet. "No."

qa.q: How late did Jaya submit her project?
qa.a: An hour late.

qa.q: What does Jaya mean by "I just hear how bad I am"?
qa.a: She feels ashamed and discouraged, and her harsh self-talk makes looking at work feel unbearable.

qa.q: What turning point does Bhupen offer?
qa.a: He suggests the harsh voice itself is the problem, inviting her to speak to herself as she would to a friend.

qa.q: What is Bhupen feeling as he sits beside her?
qa.a: Bhupen seems caring and gently worried, wanting to break her cycle of self-blame.

grounding: Shows a young woman calling herself lazy and vowing to change after a late submission, while her brother points out that harsh self-talk feeds the loop.

passage: After I submitted the lab report at 4 a.m. last month, I sat on the hostel floor and gave myself a lecture. You're lazy. You're always like this. From tomorrow, new Nirmala: timetable, early mornings, no phone. I even wrote it on a sticky note in capital letters. Two weeks later, with the next report due, I opened the file and my first thought was, here's lazy Nirmala again, about to fail again. That thought sat like a stone in my chest, and I closed the laptop just to get away from it. Varun found me at the canteen at nine that night. "Didn't you say new Nirmala?" he teased. I laughed, but inside I was saying the same cruel things, and they didn't make me start. They only made the file harder to open.

qa.q: What did Nirmala write on the sticky note?
qa.a: The vow for a new Nirmala: timetable, early mornings, no phone, in capital letters.

qa.q: Why did Nirmala close the laptop two weeks later?
qa.a: The thought of lazy Nirmala failing again left Nirmala ashamed and hopeless, a stone in the chest, and closing the laptop was a way to escape that feeling.

qa.q: What could Nirmala try instead of the harsh lecture?
qa.a: Nirmala could answer the cruel voice more kindly and aim for one small start, since the harsh talk only made the file harder to open.

qa.q: How might Varun see Nirmala's pattern?
qa.a: Varun seems to see it lightly, teasing about the new Nirmala, without knowing the cruel things Nirmala says inside.

grounding: Shows a student calling themself lazy and vowing change after a late submission, with harsh self-talk making the next task harder to face.
